title: Monte Carlo Tree Search
subtitle: Playouts, bandits, UCT and enhancements, with Python labs on Nim
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: Monte Carlo tree search from first principles (Coulom 2006; Kocsis and Szepesvari 2006; Browne et al. 2012): game trees and minimax, random playouts, multi-armed bandits and UCB1, the four steps, a complete UCT search on Nim, choosing the final move, RAVE and other enhancements, two-player perspective, and the road to AlphaGo's PUCT. Theory plus Python labs.

chapters.title: What is Monte Carlo tree search?
summary: Monte Carlo tree search, MCTS, is a way to choose good actions in a decision problem by growing a search tree guided by random simulations. It needs little domain knowledge beyond the rules.

It was developed around 2006. Remi Coulom described the idea and gave it the name. Levente Kocsis and Csaba Szepesvari proposed UCT, which uses a bandit rule to decide which branch to explore. It then transformed computer Go.
MCTS repeats four steps: selection, expansion, simulation and backpropagation. This course builds each step in small Python labs on the game of Nim.

glossary.def: Estimating a quantity by averaging random samples.
A tree whose nodes are game states and whose edges are moves.
Playing a game to the end with random or simple moves.
Upper Confidence bounds applied to Trees: MCTS with the UCB1 selection rule.
One that can be stopped at any moment and still return its best answer so far.
One pass of the four MCTS steps.

keyPoints: MCTS needs only a model of the rules: legal moves, transitions and terminal results.
Four steps per iteration: selection, expansion, simulation, backpropagation.
The tree grows towards promising moves, so it is asymmetric.
UCT (Kocsis and Szepesvari, 2006) applies the UCB1 bandit rule at every node.
Coulom (2006) used the term Monte Carlo tree search.
Browne and colleagues (2012) surveyed the method and its many variants.

items: ELI5. Monte Carlo tree search picks a move by trying lots of imagined games and remembering which first moves led to wins. Like a coach testing plays on a practice field before the real match.

Suppose you must pick a move in a game with far too many positions to search fully. Chess programs use a hand-written evaluation function to judge positions. In Go, nobody could write a good one. MCTS found another way: judge a move by playing many quick games from it and counting how often you win.

The idea has two parts. The Monte Carlo part is random sampling. Play a game to the end with random moves and see who wins. One game tells little, but the average of many tells something. The tree part is bookkeeping. Remember the results in a tree, so that more effort goes to moves that look good.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} Q(s,a) \;\approx\; \frac{1}{N(s,a)}\sum_{i=1}^{N(s,a)} z_i, \\[0.6em] z_i \in \{0, 1\}\ \text{the result of the } i\text{-th simulation} \end{gathered}

items: Credit goes to several people. Bruce Abramson in 1990 suggested estimating position values by random playouts. Remi Coulom in 2006 built these ideas into a tree search for Go and called it Monte Carlo tree search.

In the same year Levente Kocsis and Csaba Szepesvari published UCT, which supplied the missing piece: a principled rule for choosing which branch to explore. The 2012 survey by Cameron Browne and colleagues is the standard overview, and this course follows it.

MCTS has attractive properties. It needs only the rules of the game, not an evaluation function. It is anytime: stop it after one second or one hour and it still has a best move. The tree grows unevenly, deeper where moves look strong.
And with enough time its choice converges to the best move, a property proved for UCT.

It also has limits that later chapters discuss. Random playouts can be misleading, and MCTS can be fooled by traps, positions where one precise reply refutes an attractive move. AlphaGo, studied in a sister course, kept the tree but replaced random playouts by neural networks.

The labs use Nim as a test game. A pile of n stones; players alternate taking one, two or three; whoever takes the last stone wins. It is small enough to check every answer by hand, and rich enough to show every idea.

chapters.title: Games, trees and the need for search

maps.title: Game trees
links: Game tree | has | States as nodes
Branching factor | counts | Moves per state

summary: A game can be drawn as a tree. The root is the current position, each edge is a legal move, and the leaves are finished games. Solving a small game means labelling every node as a win or a loss for the player to move.

Minimax does this exactly, working up from the leaves. A position is a win if some move leads to a position that is a loss for the opponent. Minimax is perfect but needs the whole tree, which grows exponentially: with b moves per state and depth d there are about b to the d leaves.
Go has about 250 moves per position and games of 150 moves, so exact search is hopeless. That is the gap MCTS fills.

glossary.def: A tree of all positions reachable by legal play.
The average number of legal moves in a position.
Exact evaluation: you pick the best move, the opponent picks the worst for you.
A position where the game is over.

glossary.term: Win or loss for the player to move
glossary.def: The exact value of a position under perfect play.
A take-away game; here you remove 1 to 3 stones and taking the last wins.

keyPoints: Nim: take 1 to 3 stones; the player who takes the last stone wins.
A position with 0 stones is lost for the player to move: the opponent just took the last.
Minimax: win if any move leads to a loss for the opponent.
The tree has about b^d leaves; Go's b is about 250.
In Nim with a take limit of 3, positions that are multiples of 4 are lost for the player to move.
MCTS estimates what minimax computes, using samples.

items: ELI5. A game tree is every move, every reply and every reply to that, branching like a family tree. It grows so fast we cannot look at all of it, so we need to choose where to look.

Take a pile of ten stones. You and I alternate; each turn removes one, two or three; whoever takes the last stone wins. What should you do first? You could picture all possibilities: three first moves, each followed by three replies, and so on. That picture is the game tree.

Leaves are finished games. A position with no stones left means the previous player took the last stone and won, so the player to move has lost. Work backwards. A position is winning for the player to move if at least one move leads to a position that is losing for the opponent.
It is losing if every move leads to a position that is winning for the opponent.

lesson.tex: W(n) = \begin{cases} \text{lost} & n = 0 \\ \text{won} & \exists\, k \in \{1,2,3\},\ k \le n,\ W(n-k) = \text{lost} \\ \text{lost} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

items: This is minimax in its simplest form. For Nim, the answer has a pattern: a pile that is a multiple of four is lost for the player to move, since whatever you take, the opponent can take enough to leave another multiple of four. Any other pile is won: take what leaves a multiple of four.

Minimax scales badly. The number of leaves is about b to the d for b moves and depth d. Chess has b around 35 and games of about 80 plies, far beyond any computer. Go has b around 250 and about 150 plies. Chess programs cut the tree with alpha-beta pruning and an evaluation function.
For Go, no good evaluation was known.

MCTS takes a different route. It does not try to cover the tree. It samples it, and focuses the samples. In the labs below you write exact solvers for Nim first, because they give the ground truth against which the sampled estimates can be judged.

chapters.title: Random playouts and Monte Carlo estimation

maps.title: Playouts
links: Playout | plays | Random moves to the end
Error | shrinks as | One over root n
Random policy | is | Weak but unbiased

summary: A playout (also called a rollout or simulation) plays a game to the end with random moves. Its result, win or loss, is a noisy estimate of the position's value. Averaging many playouts reduces the noise.
The standard error of an average of n samples shrinks like one over the square root of n. Ten times more playouts make the estimate about three times more accurate.
The labs use a tiny linear congruential generator for pseudo-random numbers, so that every result is exactly repeatable.

glossary.def: A simulated game from a position to its end.
Wins divided by playouts.
The typical size of the estimate's error.
A deterministic formula producing numbers that look random.
Linear congruential generator: x becomes (a x + c) mod m.
The starting value of a generator.

keyPoints: The playout result for the player to move is 1 for a win and 0 for a loss.
Win rate = wins / playouts.
Standard error is about sqrt(p (1 - p) / n).
A random playout policy picks uniformly among legal moves.
Estimates from random play are noisy and may be biased as a measure of perfect-play value.
In the labs: x -> (75 x + 74) mod 65537, a small LCG, picks the move index as x mod number of moves.

items: ELI5. A random playout plays the rest of a game with random moves and notes who won. One is noisy; thousands give a fair guess. Like flipping a coin many times to judge whether it is loaded.

Take the Nim position with five stones. We know the exact answer: it is won for the player to move, by taking one stone. Pretend we do not know. We could play random games from here and count how often the player to move wins. If the estimate is above one half, the position looks good.

Each playout is a short story. Starting at the position, the player to move picks a random legal move, then the other player, and so on until the pile is empty. The one who took the last stone wins. Record 1 if that was the player who started, otherwise 0.
This is the Monte Carlo estimate and its standard error. With 100 playouts and a true rate of one half, the error is around five percentage points. With 10,000 playouts it is around half a point.
The cost grows linearly with n while the error shrinks only with its square root, a good reason to spend playouts where they matter.

There is a subtlety. The win rate under random play is not the value under perfect play. A position can be lost against a perfect opponent, yet random opponents blunder so often that it wins most playouts.
MCTS reduces this problem by choosing moves inside the tree better than randomly, so playouts are used only below the tree's frontier.

For repeatable labs we need random numbers that are reproducible. A linear congruential generator updates a number by x to (a times x plus c) modulo m. The labs use a tiny one with m of 65537, a of 75 and c of 74, so everything stays far below the integer limit.
Its quality is poor for serious work but fine for teaching.

practice.intro: Write lcg(x): the next value of the generator, (75 * x + 74) % 65537.
practice.solution:
def lcg(x):
    return (75 * x + 74) % 65537

practice.title: One random playout
practice.intro: Nim in these labs: a pile of n stones; players alternate taking 1, 2 or 3 stones; whoever takes the last stone wins. Write playout(n, seed): play random legal moves from n stones until the pile is empty. At each step: x = lcg(x) (starting from seed), the legal takes are 1..min(3, n), and the take is moves[x % len(moves)]. Return 1 if the player who moved first at the start takes the last stone, else 0. Here lcg(x) = (75 * x + 74) % 65537.
practice.hint: Alternate players; the last mover wins.
practice.solution:
def playout(n, seed):
    x = seed
    player = 0
    last = 1
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    while n > 0:
        x = (75 * x + 74) % 65537
        top = 3 if n >= 3 else n
        k = 1 + x % top
        n -= k
        last = player
        player = 1 - player
    return 1 if last == 0 else 0

practice.title: Win-rate estimate
practice.intro: Write estimate(n, k, seed): the fraction of k playouts from n stones won by the player to move. Playout j (from 0) uses the seed (seed + j) as its starting value. Same playout rule as before. Return wins / k.
practice.hint: Count playouts won by the first player.
practice.solution:
def estimate(n, k, seed):
    wins = 0
    for j in range(k):
        x = seed + j
        m = n
        player = 0
        last = 1
        if m == 0:
            continue
        while m > 0:
            x = (75 * x + 74) % 65537
            top = 3 if m >= 3 else m
            t = 1 + x % top
            m -= t
            last = player
            player = 1 - player
        if last == 0:
            wins += 1
    return wins / k

chapters.title: Bandits and the UCB1 rule

maps.title: Bandits
links: Exploitation | picks | The best known arm
Regret | measures | Loss versus the best arm

summary: A multi-armed bandit is the simplest setting where exploration and exploitation clash. There are several arms, each paying a random reward with an unknown mean. You pull one arm per round and want the highest total reward.

UCB1, by Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer in 2002, picks the arm with the highest upper confidence bound: its average reward plus a bonus that is large for rarely pulled arms. Its regret grows only logarithmically with the number of pulls.
In MCTS, each move at each node is an arm and each playout is a pull.

glossary.def: A problem of repeatedly choosing among arms with unknown reward distributions.
Choosing the arm that has looked best so far.
Choosing an arm to learn about it.
Choose the arm maximising mean + c sqrt(2 ln N / n_i).
The reward lost by not always playing the best arm.
The term that grows when an arm has been tried few times.

keyPoints: UCB1 value of arm i: mean_i + c * sqrt(2 ln N / n_i).
N is the total number of pulls and n_i the pulls of arm i; untried arms are pulled first.
The bonus shrinks as n_i grows and grows slowly as N grows, so every arm is revisited eventually.
UCB1 has logarithmic regret in the number of pulls (Auer et al., 2002).
In UCT the constant is written C_p; the survey notes 1/sqrt(2) for rewards in [0, 1].
In MCTS the arm is a child move; the reward is a playout result.

items: ELI5. A bandit is a row of slot machines where you do not know which pays best. UCB1 says: try the ones that look good, but also the ones you have barely tried. It balances greed with curiosity.

Imagine a row of slot machines. Each pays out on average a different amount, which you do not know. You have a thousand coins. If you pull each once and then stick with the best looking one, you may be fooled by luck. If you keep trying all of them, you waste coins on poor machines.
How do you balance?

UCB1 gives a clean answer. Give each arm a score equal to its average reward so far plus a bonus. The bonus is big when the arm has been pulled rarely, because the average is then unreliable, and small when it has been pulled many times. Always pull the arm with the highest score.
This is optimism in the face of uncertainty.

Look at the bonus. As n i grows the bonus falls, so well-sampled arms must earn their place with their average. As the total N grows, ln N grows slowly, so a neglected arm's bonus rises until it is tried again. No arm is dropped forever.
Auer and colleagues proved that the total regret grows only logarithmically in the number of pulls, which is the best order possible.

The constant c sets the balance. In the original analysis for rewards between zero and one, c is one. The MCTS survey writes the constant for UCT as C p and notes the value one over the square root of two satisfies the theory for rewards in the unit interval. In practice it is tuned.
Larger values explore more.
The labs write the UCB1 score, choose the best arm, and measure regret in a small deterministic bandit.

chapters.title: The four steps: selection, expansion, simulation, backpropagation

maps.title: One iteration
links: Selection | descends | Using a tree policy

summary: Each iteration starts at the root. Selection walks down through nodes already in the tree, following a tree policy. When it reaches a node with an untried move, expansion adds a child for one. Simulation plays from the new node to the end with a default policy.
Backpropagation then updates every node on the path with the result.
Each node stores two numbers: its visit count N and its total reward W. The mean reward is W over N.
Because the players alternate, the result must be flipped as it travels up: a win for one player is a loss for the other.

glossary.def: The rule used to pick children while inside the tree.
The rule used to play moves in the simulation, often random.
How many iterations passed through a node.
The sum of results backed up through a node.
A legal move with no child node yet.
The boundary between the tree and the unexplored part.

keyPoints: Selection: from the root, follow the tree policy to a node that is not fully expanded or is terminal.
Expansion: add one child for an untried move.
Simulation: play the default policy from the new child to a terminal state.
Backpropagation: add 1 to N on every node of the path, and add the result to W from that node's perspective.
Rewards from a node's parent's perspective alternate with depth.
After the iterations, the move is chosen from the root's children.

items: ELI5. Each round has four steps: walk down the tree by the best looking path, add a new node, play randomly to the end, then update the scores back up the path.
MCTS grows a tree one node per iteration. Each iteration is the same four-step cycle, and the cycle is the heart of the algorithm. Learn it well and the rest is variation.

Selection. Start at the root, the current position. If the node is fully expanded, which means every legal move already has a child, pick a child with the tree policy and move down. Repeat until you reach a node that has an untried move, or a finished game.
Expansion. If the node has an untried move, create the child for it and add it to the tree. Only one node is added per iteration, which keeps the tree growing slowly and evenly.
Simulation. From the new node, play the game to the end with the default policy. In plain MCTS the default policy is uniformly random. The final result is recorded: win, loss or perhaps a score.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} N(v) \leftarrow N(v) + 1, \\[0.6em] W(v) \leftarrow W(v) + r_v \\[0.6em] \text{for every node } v \text{ on the path} \end{gathered}

items: Backpropagation. Walk back up the path from the new node to the root. Add one to each node's visit count and add the result to its total. Take care of perspective. In a two-player game the result that is good for the player who made the move into a node is bad for the player moving out of it.

So the reward alternates between one and zero down the path. Many programs store at each node the result from the viewpoint of the player who moved into it, so the selection at the parent can simply maximise.
The loop then repeats, thousands or millions of times. The visit counts concentrate on strong moves, and the final choice reads them off. The labs implement each step on a small tree stored in lists.

practice.title: Backpropagate
practice.intro: A path is a list of nodes from the root down to the new node, each node a [visits, total] pair. Write backprop(path, result): add 1 to the visits of each node and add the result to the total of the new (last) node, alternating the result between result and 1 - result going up the path (the last node gets result, its parent gets 1 - result, and so on). Return the updated path.
practice.hint: Count back from the last node to decide the sign.
practice.solution:
def backprop(path, result):
    out = []
    n = len(path)
    for i in range(n):
        steps = n - 1 - i
        r = result if steps % 2 == 0 else 1 - result
        out.append([path[i][0] + 1, path[i][1] + r])
    return out

practice.hint: Legal moves minus those with children.

chapters.title: UCT and a complete search

maps.title: UCT
links: UCT | applies | UCB1 in the tree
Child score | is | Mean plus bonus
Best move | is | Most visited child

summary: UCT is MCTS with UCB1 as the tree policy: at each node, descend to the child maximising its mean reward plus an exploration bonus. This treats every node as a bandit problem.
With the pieces from earlier chapters we can write a full search. Run a fixed number of iterations from the current position, then play the root move with the most visits.
The labs do exactly that on Nim, with a small deterministic random generator, so the whole search is repeatable.

glossary.def: mean + C sqrt(ln N_parent / n_child), in the survey's form with a constant.
The number of iterations or the time allowed.
The move chosen from the root after the search.
The child with the highest visit count.
A node with a child for every legal move.
With enough iterations UCT's choice approaches the optimal move.

keyPoints: UCT picks the child maximising mean + C * sqrt(ln(N_parent) / n_child).
Browne et al. write the bonus as 2 C_p sqrt(2 ln n / n_j); the constants differ only by scaling C.
Kocsis and Szepesvari proved that UCT converges to the minimax value for finite games.
Choose the final move by visits.
More iterations give better play.
The labs fix C = 1 and a deterministic generator.

items: ELI5. UCT is MCTS using UCB1 inside the tree. As more rounds run, the tree grows toward the best lines and ignores hopeless ones. It gets better the longer it thinks.

Now we assemble the full algorithm. At each node reached in selection that has all its moves tried, use the UCT rule to choose among its children. Where it has untried moves, expand one. Then simulate and back up.

The survey writes the rule with a factor of two and a constant C p, but the shape is the same: the first term favours moves that did well, the second favours moves tried little. The constant C is tuned for the game.
A larger C explores more and may waste simulations; a smaller C exploits more and may miss good moves.

Kocsis and Szepesvari proved a strong property: for finite games, with enough iterations the probability of choosing a suboptimal move goes to zero, so UCT converges to the minimax answer. The result is asymptotic.
In practice the number of iterations needed can be very large, particularly in games with traps.

How to pick the move at the end? The most robust choice is the child with the most visits, since a high visit count means UCT kept finding it worth exploring. The child with the highest mean can be a lucky sample with few visits. Chapter 7 compares the options.

Because the search tree carries over, a program can keep the subtree of the move actually played and reuse its statistics on the next turn. And because the search is anytime, the program can think for as long as the clock allows.

practice.title: Full UCT search on Nim
practice.intro: Nim in these labs: a pile of n stones; players alternate taking 1, 2 or 3 stones; whoever takes the last stone wins. Write uct_nim(n, iterations, c, seed): run UCT from a pile of n stones. Each node stores visits N and total W from the viewpoint of the player who made the move INTO it (so at the parent we maximise W/N). Selection: at a node with an untried take, expand the smallest untried take; otherwise choose the child by w/n + c*sqrt(ln(parent N)/n) (ties to the lowest take). Simulation: random playout with x = (75*x + 74) % 65537, take = 1 + x % min(3, pile), x continuing across iterations (start at seed). Backpropagate alternating perspective. Return the take with the most visits at the root (ties to the lowest). For a terminal node (pile 0) the player who moved into it won (result 1 for that node).
practice.hint: Follow the description exactly; the same generator makes it repeatable.
practice.solution:
import math
def uct_nim(n, iterations, c, seed):
    # node: [pile, visits, total, children dict take->node]
    root = [n, 0, 0.0, {}]
    x = seed
    for it in range(iterations):
        node = root
        path = [node]
        # selection and expansion
        while node[0] > 0:
            top = 3 if node[0] >= 3 else node[0]
            untried = None
            for k in range(1, top + 1):
                if k not in node[3]:
                    untried = k
                    break
            if untried is not None:
                child = [node[0] - untried, 0, 0.0, {}]
                node[3][untried] = child
                node = child
                path.append(node)
                break
            best = -1e18
            arg = 1
            for k in range(1, top + 1):
                ch = node[3][k]
                s = ch[2] / ch[1] + c * math.sqrt(math.log(max(node[1], 1)) / ch[1])
                if s > best + 1e-12:
                    best = s
                    arg = k
            node = node[3][arg]
            path.append(node)
        # simulation: result for the player who moved into the last node
        pile = node[0]
        if pile == 0:
            r = 1
        else:
            mover = 1  # 1 = the player to move at the node (not the one who moved into it)
            last = 0
            while pile > 0:
                x = (75 * x + 74) % 65537
                top = 3 if pile >= 3 else pile
                pile -= 1 + x % top
                last = mover
                mover = 1 - mover
            # last == 1 means the player to move at the node took the last stone
            r = 0 if last == 1 else 1
        for i in range(len(path) - 1, -1, -1):
            path[i][1] += 1
            path[i][2] += r
            r = 1 - r
    best = -1
    arg = 1
    for k in sorted(root[3].keys()):
        if root[3][k][1] > best:
            best = root[3][k][1]
            arg = k
    return arg

chapters.title: Choosing the final move

maps.title: Final move
links: Secure child | maximises | A lower bound
Most visits | is | The usual choice

summary: After the iterations, the program must pick a move from the root's children. The survey lists several criteria. The max child has the highest mean reward. The robust child has the highest visit count. The max-robust child is the one with both, and if none exists the search continues.
The secure child maximises a lower confidence bound.
The mean of a barely visited child is unreliable: a single lucky playout can make it look perfect. Visit counts are steadier, so the robust child is the usual choice.
The labs implement each criterion and show where they disagree.

glossary.def: The child with the highest mean reward.
The child with the most visits.
A child that is both max and robust.
The child maximising mean minus a multiple of its standard error.
A pessimistic estimate: mean minus a margin.
A fixed rule for equal scores.

keyPoints: Robust child: argmax visits.
Max child: argmax mean.
Secure child: argmax of mean - A / sqrt(n) for a constant A.
A child with 1 visit and mean 1.0 is not trustworthy.
UCT concentrates visits on good moves, so max and robust usually agree after many iterations.
Disagreement signals that more iterations are needed.

items: ELI5. At the end, pick the move that was visited most, not the one with the highest average. Many visits mean the search came back to it again and again. It is the more robust choice.
Suppose the search ends with three candidate moves. Move A: 900 visits, mean 0.62. Move B: 80 visits, mean 0.70. Move C: 3 visits, mean 1.00. Which to play?

The max child is C, with the highest mean. But three playouts prove little: the true win rate could be well below one half. The robust child is A, the most visited. UCT only keeps visiting a move while it looks competitive, so a large visit count is evidence that the move held up under pressure.
A is the usual choice.

The secure child penalises uncertainty explicitly. Subtract from the mean a margin that shrinks with the number of visits. With a suitable A, move C is penalised heavily and move A scores best again. The survey mentions this among the options and describes the bound as a lower confidence bound.

When max and robust children differ, a common remedy is to keep searching until they agree, which is the idea behind the max-robust child. Some programs extend the thinking time when the best move is unclear, and cut it short when it is obvious.

A last practical point is ties. Several children can have the same visit count, particularly in short searches. Pick by a fixed rule such as the highest mean, then the lowest index, so that behaviour is repeatable.

chapters.title: Enhancements: RAVE, priors, widening and more

maps.title: Variants
links: RAVE | shares | Move statistics across the tree
AMAF | counts | Moves played anywhere later
Progressive widening | limits | Children by visits

summary: Plain UCT is slow to learn in big games. The survey describes many enhancements. All-moves-as-first, AMAF, and its tree version RAVE share information between positions: a move that did well when played later in a playout is probably good now.

Other ideas: give unvisited children a first-play urgency value; widen the set of considered moves gradually as the node gets more visits; use domain knowledge or a policy to bias playouts; merge identical positions in a transposition table; and run many threads using virtual loss.
These are from the survey and later work; the labs implement three of the simplest.

glossary.def: All moves as first: credit a move when it appears anywhere later in the playout.
Rapid Action Value Estimation: blends AMAF and ordinary statistics in the tree.
A value assigned to unvisited children in place of infinity.
Allow only a growing number of children as the parent's visits increase.
Different move orders reaching the same position.
A temporary penalty that steers parallel threads to different branches.

keyPoints: AMAF/RAVE: from Gelly and Silver's work on Go, described in the survey.
RAVE blends: beta * AMAF mean + (1 - beta) * ordinary mean, with beta falling as visits grow.
First-play urgency: unvisited children get a fixed score instead of infinity.
Progressive widening: allowed children = ceil(k * visits^alpha).
Heuristic or learned playout policies play better than uniform random.
Parallelisation: tree parallelism with virtual loss, leaf or root parallelism.

items: ELI5. Enhancements add hints: share what is learned across similar moves, give moves starting scores, or look at fewer branches. They speed up learning when the search has little time.

Plain UCT treats every position separately. In Go, with hundreds of moves, a large number of playouts is needed before any move has enough statistics. The enhancements make better use of each playout.

All-moves-as-first is the best known idea. In a playout, a move that appears later may have helped even though it was not played at the root. AMAF credits every move that either side played later in the playout, as though it had been played first.
This gives many more samples per move, though noisier ones. RAVE combines the AMAF estimate with the ordinary estimate, trusting AMAF early and the ordinary mean as visits accumulate.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} Q_{\mathrm{RAVE}}(a) \;=\; \beta\, Q_{\mathrm{AMAF}}(a) + (1-\beta)\, Q(a), \\[0.6em] \beta \text{ falls as } N(a) \text{ grows} \end{gathered}

items: The unvisited-children rule matters too. Plain UCT gives an unvisited child an infinite score, so every child is tried once before any is tried twice. With 250 moves that costs 250 playouts at every node.
First-play urgency instead gives an unvisited child a fixed value, so a good known move can be revisited before all the others are tried.

Progressive widening handles very large or continuous move sets. At first only a few children are allowed. As the parent's visit count rises, more are allowed, usually in proportion to a power of the visit count. The best-looking moves, by a heuristic, are added first.

Domain knowledge helps in playouts. Instead of uniformly random moves, a heuristic policy might prefer captures or local replies. A stronger default policy gives better estimates, though not always: the survey notes that a stronger playout policy does not guarantee a stronger search.
Later systems replaced playouts with learned value estimates. That is the step AlphaGo took.

Finally, parallelism. Several threads can share the tree. Virtual loss temporarily counts a visit as a loss on the path being explored, which discourages other threads from following it. The labs implement an AMAF update, first-play urgency and progressive widening.

import math
def rave_value(q_amaf, q_tree, n, k):
    beta = math.sqrt(k / (3 * n + k))
    return beta * q_amaf + (1 - beta) * q_tree

chapters.title: Two players, perspective and heuristics
summary: Two-player games need care with perspective. A node should store results from the viewpoint of the player who moved into it, and the reward flips at every level. Draws score one half.
MCTS is often seen as a selective, sampled version of minimax: the mean values in the tree approach minimax values, while the tree grows deeper along strong lines.
Compared with alpha-beta, MCTS shines when evaluation functions are hard to write and branching is large; alpha-beta shines when a good evaluation function exists and tactics are narrow.

glossary.def: The player from whose viewpoint a reward is measured.
A form of minimax where each level negates the value.
A pruning method that skips branches that cannot affect the minimax result.
A hand-written estimate of a position's value.
A reward scaled into the range 0 to 1.
A position where one precise move refutes an attractive line.

keyPoints: Win = 1, draw = 0.5, loss = 0 from the perspective of the player who moved into the node.
Backup: r for the leaf's mover; 1 - r for the other player, alternating.
MCTS needs no evaluation function; alpha-beta usually does.
Alpha-beta prunes exactly; MCTS focuses statistically.
MCTS can be weak in narrow tactical lines with traps.
Hybrid systems exist; AlphaGo-style systems mix MCTS with learned networks.

items: ELI5. In a two-player game, a good move for me is a bad move for you. The scores flip with each turn. Heuristics can also replace the random playout with a smarter guess.

In a two-player game, one side's gain is the other's loss. That structure has to be respected in the tree. At a node where the opponent is to move, the opponent will pick the child that is best for them, which is worst for us.
If the node stores the result from the viewpoint of whoever moved into it, the choice at the parent is always a plain maximisation over children, one level at a time.

This is the zero-sum symmetry. With scores that are not wins and losses, such as points, the common approach is to scale them into the range zero to one so that the same bandit rule applies, and to treat a draw as one half.

How does MCTS relate to the classical alternative? Alpha-beta search explores the game tree to a fixed depth with pruning, then calls an evaluation function. Its results are exact for that depth. MCTS explores unevenly, with no fixed depth, and uses playouts in place of an evaluation function.
Its values are statistical. The tree-wide averages tend to minimax values as iterations grow.

Which is better depends on the game. Chess has good hand-made evaluation functions and many narrow tactical lines, a good fit for alpha-beta. Go has huge branching and no good evaluation function, a good fit for MCTS. Where lines are very narrow, a single refutation can be missed by sampling.
The survey describes such trap states as a weakness of plain MCTS.
Bias in the playouts is a further risk. If the default policy is biased, so are the estimates. Domain knowledge can help and can also hurt.

A broader point: since 2016, programs such as AlphaGo and AlphaZero keep the MCTS tree but evaluate leaves with neural networks and steer selection with a learned policy, as described in the sister courses.

chapters.title: Applications, limits and where it leads

maps.title: Beyond games
links: MCTS | used in | General game playing
MCTS | used in | Planning and scheduling

summary: MCTS was the breakthrough behind the strong Go programs of 2006 to 2015 and then became a general tool: in video games, general game playing, planning, scheduling and optimisation problems. The survey lists applications across games and non-game domains.
It has weak spots. Traps can fool it; very long games with sparse rewards give little signal; the cost per iteration limits depth. Remedies include better playouts, learned priors and learned values.
The modern line of work, AlphaGo, AlphaZero and MuZero, keeps the tree search and replaces random playouts by learned networks.

glossary.def: Playing any game given only its rules.
A signal that appears only at the very end.
A UCT variant that adds a prior probability from a neural network.
A system that also learns a model of the environment for the search.
Choosing actions by looking ahead in a model.
A neural network estimate of a position's value, used instead of a playout.

keyPoints: Go programs using MCTS reached strong amateur level before 2015.
The survey covers games and non-game domains such as planning and scheduling.
Weaknesses: traps, long sparse-reward horizons, memory growth.
PUCT adds a policy prior to the selection rule.
AlphaGo (2016) and AlphaZero (2017) combine MCTS with deep networks.
MCTS needs a model of the environment, or a learned one as in MuZero.

items: ELI5. MCTS suits problems with a simulator and a hard-to-score position. It is the base of AlphaGo and many planners. It struggles when random play tells you nothing.

Before 2006, the best Go programs played at the level of a modest club player. With MCTS, programs climbed to strong amateur level within a few years, long before neural networks were available, which is why the method became famous. It was the first reliable way to handle the huge branching of Go.

The method spread. General game playing programs, which are given only the rules of a new game, adopted it because it needs no hand-made evaluation. Video games, planning problems, scheduling and optimisation tasks followed, as the survey documents.
Wherever you have a simulator and a decision tree, MCTS is a candidate.

It has limits you should know. Traps, as in chapter 9, can be missed. When a game is long and the only reward comes at the end, random playouts have little signal. Each iteration costs a playout, so depth is limited. And memory grows with the tree.
Remedies include better default policies, domain heuristics and early cut-offs with an evaluation.

lesson.tex: a^{*} \;=\; \arg\max_a \left( Q(s,a) + c\, P(s,a)\,\frac{\sqrt{\sum_b N(s,b)}}{1 + N(s,a)} \right)

items: The formula above is PUCT, the selection rule of AlphaGo and AlphaZero: the exploration bonus is scaled by a prior probability P from a policy network, so the search tries promising moves first. Leaves are scored by a value network instead of a random playout.
The tree, the four steps and the visit-count choice stay. That is why knowing MCTS makes those systems easy to read.

MuZero goes one step further by learning the model of the environment as well, so that the tree can search where the rules are not given. You will find the details in the courses on AlphaGo and AlphaZero in this library.
Where to go next: read the Browne survey for the long list of variants, implement MCTS for a game of your choice such as tic-tac-toe or Connect Four, and compare it with your own alpha-beta program.
In the labs, you will build the pieces of the PUCT rule, measure tree statistics and write a simple tournament.
